payload.text: Layering works like posting a parcel abroad. You write the letter, the post office adds an address label, the airline adds its own tracking tag, and each handler reads only the label meant for them. Nobody at the airport opens your letter, just as a router never reads the web page inside a packet.

section.heading: Finding the layer of an attack

payload.text:
To place an attack on the model, ask what the attacker tampers with:

- the signal on the wire or in the air: layer 1
- frames and local (MAC) addresses: layer 2
- packets and IP addresses: layer 3
- ports and connections: layer 4
- sessions and encryption: layers 5 and 6
- the application's own data and logic: layer 7

The defence usually works at the same layer. A firewall that only checks IP addresses and ports (layers 3 and 4) lets a SQL injection through, because the attack sits in layer 7 data that such a firewall never reads. That is why defenders stack controls at several layers, which is called **defence in depth**.

rows.label: 3 Network

rows.label: 2 Data link

rows.label: 1 Physical
values: Tapping or jamming the cable or radio

payload.text: Think of every attack as tampering with one layer's envelope. Find the envelope the attacker touched, and you know which layer to defend first, and which defences (a firewall, TLS, a switch setting) can see the attack at all.
